claim: Deciding how difficult it is going to be to perform a task allows us to choose between tasks.
source: Deciding how difficult it is going to be to perform a task allows us to choose between tasks, allocate appropriate resources, and predict future performance.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract without specific experimental data, but is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deciding how difficult it is going to be to perform a task allows us to allocate appropriate resources.
source: Deciding how difficult it is going to be to perform a task allows us to choose between tasks, allocate appropriate resources, and predict future performance.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract without specific experimental data, but is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deciding how difficult it is going to be to perform a task allows us to predict future performance.
source: Deciding how difficult it is going to be to perform a task allows us to choose between tasks, allocate appropriate resources, and predict future performance.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract without specific experimental data, but is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: To be useful for planning, difficulty judgments should not require completion of the task.
source: To be useful for planning, difficulty judgments should not require completion of the task.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the utility of prospective difficulty judgments.

claim: Participants viewed two patches of dynamic random dots, which were colored blue or yellow stochastically on each appearance.
source: Participants viewed two patches of dynamic random dots, which were colored blue or yellow stochastically on each appearance.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Stimulus coherence (the probability, pblue, of a dot being blue) varied across trials and patches thus establishing difficulty, |pblue −0.5|.
source: Stimulus coherence (the probability, pblue, of a dot being blue) varied across trials and patches thus establishing difficulty, |pblue −0.5|.
evidence: This describes how difficulty was operationalized in the experimental design.

claim: Accuracy in difficulty decisions improved with the difference in the stimulus difficulties.
source: Accuracy in difficulty decisions improved with the difference in the stimulus difficulties, whereas the reaction times were not determined solely by this quantity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Reaction times were not determined solely by the difference in stimulus difficulties.
source: Accuracy in difficulty decisions improved with the difference in the stimulus difficulties, whereas the reaction times were not determined solely by this quantity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: When the patches shared the same difficulty, reaction times were shorter for easier stimuli.
source: For example, when the patches shared the same difficulty, reaction times were shorter for easier stimuli.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data demonstrating the magnitude effect.

claim: Participants compare the absolute accumulated evidence from each stimulus and terminate their decision when they differed by a set amount.
source: A comparison of several models of difficulty judgment suggested that participants compare the absolute accumulated evidence from each stimulus and terminate their decision when they differed by a set amount.
evidence: This is the conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: When the dominant color of each stimulus is known, reaction times should depend only on the difference in difficulty.
source: The model predicts that when the dominant color of each stimulus is known, reaction times should depend only on the difference in difficulty, which we confirm empirically.
evidence: This is a model prediction that was tested and confirmed experimentally.

claim: The difference model is preferred to one that compares the confidence one would have in making each decision.
source: We also show that this model is preferred to one that compares the confidence one would have in making each decision.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: Estimating the difficulty of different tasks allows us to decide which task to engage in.
source: Estimating the difficulty of different tasks we might perform allows us to decide which task to engage in Bennett-Pierre et al., 2018; Wisniewski et al., 2015, allocate the necessary amount of effort or cognitive control (Shenhav et al., 2013; Dunn et al., 2019), and predict our ability to perform the task successfully (Morgan et al., 2014; Siedlecka et al., 2016; Fleming et al., 2016, Moskowitz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Estimating the difficulty of different tasks allows us to allocate the necessary amount of effort or cognitive control.
source: Estimating the difficulty of different tasks we might perform allows us to decide which task to engage in Bennett-Pierre et al., 2018; Wisniewski et al., 2015, allocate the necessary amount of effort or cognitive control (Shenhav et al., 2013; Dunn et al., 2019), and predict our ability to perform the task successfully (Morgan et al., 2014; Siedlecka et al., 2016; Fleming et al., 2016, Moskowitz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Estimating the difficulty of different tasks allows us to predict our ability to perform the task successfully.
source: Estimating the difficulty of different tasks we might perform allows us to decide which task to engage in Bennett-Pierre et al., 2018; Wisniewski et al., 2015, allocate the necessary amount of effort or cognitive control (Shenhav et al., 2013; Dunn et al., 2019), and predict our ability to perform the task successfully (Morgan et al., 2014; Siedlecka et al., 2016; Fleming et al., 2016, Moskowitz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Past studies of difficulty judgments have mainly relied on complex tasks.
source: Past studies of difficulty judgments have mainly relied on complex tasks, like five-grade students judging the difficulty of remembering a sentence (Stein et al., 1982) or physics teachers evaluating the difficulty of different exam questions (Fakcharoenphol et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cues and heuristics play an important role in estimating task difficulty.
source: This line of research highlights the important role that cues and heuristics play in estimating task difficulty (Vangsness and Young, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The complexity of naturalistic tasks precludes quantitative modeling and identification of the inference process underlying the formation of difficulty judgments.
source: While the use of complex naturalistic tasks ensures that difficulty estimates are realistic, their complexity precludes quantitative modeling and thus the identification of the inference process underlying the formation of difficulty judgments.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of prior research approaches.

claim: Decision confidence is often defined as the probability that a choice, just made, is correct or appropriate.
source: Decision confidence is often defined as the probability that a choice, just made, is correct or appropriate (Peirce and Jastrow, 1884; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Confidence in a decision one has made can be converted to difficulty (the signal-to-noise ratio) if one knows how long it took to reach the decision.
source: In fact, confidence in a decision one has made can be converted to difficulty (the signal-to-noise ratio) if one knows how long it took to reach the decision (Kiani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Difficulty estimation can be prospective or retrospective, and can even be independent of task performance.
source: Difficulty estimation can be prospective or retrospective, and can even be independent of task performance (Desender et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Judgments of difficulty obey a sequential sampling process similar to one that would be used to make a single decision about perceptual category.
source: Our results show that judgments of difficulty obey a sequential sampling process similar to one that would be used to make a single decision about perceptual category.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data and modeling.

claim: Difficulty judgments rely on tracking the difference in the absolute accumulated evidence for color judgments for the two stimuli.
source: However, rather than accumulating evidence for color, difficulty judgments rely on tracking the difference in the absolute accumulated evidence for color judgments for the two stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data and modeling.

claim: Participants' choices and RTs varied according to color strength in the color judgment task.
source: Participants' choices and RTs varied according to color strength.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Participants chose the correct color more often when the strength increased.
source: As expected, participants chose the correct color more often, and they responded faster, when the strength increased.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Participants responded faster when the color strength increased.
source: As expected, participants chose the correct color more often, and they responded faster, when the strength increased.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The color judgment data are well described by a standard drift diffusion model.
source: The data are well described by a standard drift diffusion model (black lines) that explains the choice and RT by applying a stopping bound to the accumulation of the noisy color evidence (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a conclusion from model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: Participants chose S1 more often with increasing strength of S1 and decreasing strength of S2 in the difficulty judgment task.
source: Participants chose S1 more often with increasing strength of S1 (Figure 1d top, abscissa) and decreasing strength of S2, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: RTs tend to be slowest when the strength of both stimuli are the same in the difficulty judgment task.
source: For a given S1 strength (Figure 1d bottom, abscissa), RTs tend to be slowest when the strength of both stimuli are the same (open symbols), and the RTs accompanying these same matched difficulties are shorter for higher strength (Figure 1d bottom, inset).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: RTs accompanying matched difficulties are shorter for higher strength in the difficulty judgment task.
source: For a given S1 strength (Figure 1d bottom, abscissa), RTs tend to be slowest when the strength of both stimuli are the same (open symbols), and the RTs accompanying these same matched difficulties are shorter for higher strength (Figure 1d bottom, inset).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: RTs are not simply a function of the difference between the two strengths in the difficulty judgment task.
source: Therefore, the RTs are not simply a function of the difference between the two strengths.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Evidence accumulation models have been very successful in explaining choice, RT, and even confidence in many perceptual and mnemonic decision tasks, including color discrimination.
source: This is a reasonable assumption because these models have been very successful in explaining choice, RT, and even confidence in many perceptual and mnemonic decision tasks, including color discrimination (Bakkour et al., 2019; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: All models assume that for each stimulus (S1 and S2), momentary color evidence (MCE) for blue vs. yellow (positive for blue) is extracted at each point in time.
source: All models assume that for each stimulus (S1 and S2), momentary color evidence (MCE) for blue vs. yellow (positive for blue) is extracted at each point in time.
evidence: This is a common assumption across all models tested.

claim: The difference model was the preferred model for 12 out of 20 participants.
source: Compared to all other models, the difference model was the preferred model for 12 out of 20 participants (Figure 3, bottom row).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The race model fails to capture the crossing of RTs for easy-easy vs. easy-hard stimuli.
source: The race model fails to capture the crossing of RTs for easy-easy vs. easy-hard stimuli since it predicts that decisions are fastest when both stimuli are easy.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: The absolute momentary evidence model underestimates RTs when both stimuli are hard.
source: However, it underestimates RTs when both stimuli are hard.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: The fits obtained with the difference model and two-step model were very similar, and both provided a good fit to participants' data.
source: Finally, the fits obtained with the difference model and two-step model were very similar, and both provided a good fit to participants' data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: The two-step model requires an extra parameter for the initial color bound compared to the difference model.
source: However, the two-step model requires an extra parameter for the initial color bound.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The difference model was the preferred model for 14 out of 20 participants compared to the two-step model.
source: Consequently, compared to the two-step model, the difference model was the preferred model for 14 out of 20 participants.
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: The two-step model becomes identical to the difference model if the color dominance of each patch is known.
source: Note that the two-step model becomes identical to the difference model if the color dominance of each patch is known, obviating the need for the first step of the model.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the model structure.

claim: The RTs depend on more than the difference in strengths in the unknown color condition.
source: This way of plotting the RT highlights the fact that the RTs depend on more than the difference in strengths (i.e., also the strengths of S2, colors).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data in Experiment 2.

claim: There is a striking, qualitative difference in the pattern of RTs between known and unknown color conditions.
source: However, there is a striking, qualitative difference in the pattern of RTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the experimental data in the two conditions.

claim: The RTs appear to depend only on the difference in strengths in the known color condition.
source: Consistent with prediction, the RTs appear to depend only on the difference in strengths (Figure 5b, bottom right), and they are faster when the color dominance is known (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data in Experiment 2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: RTs are faster when the color dominance is known.
source: Consistent with prediction, the RTs appear to depend only on the difference in strengths (Figure 5b, bottom right), and they are faster when the color dominance is known (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data in Experiment 2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: Similar bounds are used in the unknown and known color conditions as accuracy is similar.
source: Taken together, this suggests that similar bounds are used in the unknown and known color conditions as accuracy is similar.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In the unknown color condition it takes longer, on average, to reach the bound leading to longer RTs.
source: However, in the unknown color condition it takes longer, on average, to reach the bound (as in Figure 4a vs. Figure 4b) leading to longer RTs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and model predictions.

claim: In the difference model the decision only depends on the difference in the two DVs and not on the level of either DV.
source: In the difference model the decision only depends on the difference in the two DVs and not on the level of either DV.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: In the confidence model, the difference in confidence depends on the difference in DVs as well as the actual level of each DV.
source: In contrast, the difference in confidence depends on the difference in DVs as well as the actual level of each DV.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Confidence increases supra-linearly with DV.
source: Indeed, confidence increases supra-linearly with DV such that a 0.64:0.64 coherence trial will tend to have a bigger difference in confidence than a 0:0 trial, which would lead to much shorter RTs for the former.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about confidence computations.

claim: Accuracy improved with longer stimulus durations in the controlled duration task.
source: As expected, accuracy improved with longer stimulus durations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data in the controlled duration task.

claim: Knowing the correct color improves the accuracy and speed of difficulty judgments despite the fact that color identity is not relevant for the final difficulty choice.
source: In summary, Experiment 2 provides evidence that knowing the correct color improves the accuracy and speed of difficulty judgments despite the fact that color identity is not relevant for the final difficulty choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data in Experiment 2.

claim: When the correct color is known, difficulty judgments are based on a comparison of appropriately signed DVs, which provide more information than the unsigned absolute strength of evidence.
source: This effect is explained by the difference model: when the correct color is known, difficulty judgments are based on a comparison of appropriately signed DVs, which provide more information than the unsigned absolute strength of evidence, as explained above.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the model structure and experimental findings.

claim: Behavior derived from the optimal decision policy is qualitatively similar to that of the participants for the unknown color dominance condition.
source: For the unknown color dominance condition (Experiment 1) behavior derived from the optimal decision policy (see Materials and methods) is qualitatively similar to that of the participants (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the optimal model simulations to experimental data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The optimal model captures the crossing of RTs for easy-easy vs. easy-hard stimuli.
source: The optimal model also captures the crossing of RTs for easy-easy vs. easy-hard stimuli that we observed in the data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the optimal model simulations to experimental data.

claim: At early times, the decision space of the optimal model resembles that of the difference model.
source: At early times, the decision space resembles that of the difference model, in that the decision variable can diffuse along four paths defined by the possible signs of the color coherences.
evidence: This is a conclusion from analyzing the optimal model's decision space.

claim: Later in a trial, the regions where it is optimal to continue sampling evidence become disjoint in the optimal model.
source: However, later in a trial, the regions where it is optimal to continue sampling evidence become disjoint.
evidence: This is a conclusion from analyzing the optimal model's decision space.

claim: The optimal model for the known color RT condition was in qualitative agreement with the experimental data.
source: The optimal model was in qualitative agreement with the experimental data (Figure 8c) and its bounds (Figure 8d) are similar to the difference model.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the optimal model simulations to experimental data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Response times in the optimal model for known color were largely determined by the difference between the coherences.
source: Response times were largely determined by the difference between the coherences, such that RTs were faster when the absolute value of difference was higher.
evidence: This is a conclusion from analyzing the optimal model simulations.

claim: In the optimal model for known color, the RTs also depended on the absolute value of the coherences, such that coherences closer to the extremes of the range led to faster RTs.
source: However, there is a notable exception. In contrast to what we observed in the experimental data, the RTs of the optimal model also depended on the absolute value of the coherences, such that coherences closer to the extremes of the range led to faster RTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from analyzing the optimal model simulations.

claim: The optimal model—but not the participants—seems to exploit the knowledge of the distribution over coherences to make better decisions.
source: The optimal model—but not the participants—seems to exploit the knowledge of the distribution over coherences to make better decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the optimal model to participant behavior.

claim: In some cases, the difficulty decision is made faster than at least one of the perceptual decisions.
source: In some cases, the difficulty decision is made faster than at least one of the perceptual decisions (e.g., the difficult perceptual decision when the other stimulus is very easy).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The difficulty judgment does not require completion of the color decisions.
source: Thus, the difficulty judgment does not require completion of the color decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Making a color choice for 0% color strength takes longer than a difficulty choice for 0:0.52 color strengths.
source: For example, making a color choice for 0% color strength takes longer than a difficulty choice for 0:0.52 color strengths.
evidence: This is a specific example from the experimental data.

claim: In other cases, the two perceptual decisions are almost certainly completed before the difficulty decision.
source: However, in other cases, the two perceptual decisions are almost certainly completed before the difficulty decision (e.g., when color decisions are both very easy).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Comparative judgments of difficulty allow us to ignore participant-specific attributes of the estimation.
source: Moreover, comparative judgments of difficulty allow us to ignore participant-specific attributes of the estimation (e.g., a task may be more difficult for one participant than for another one), and the idiosyncrasies involved in mapping a subjective quantity to a numeric scale (Mamassian, 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by a citation.

claim: The model makes concrete the idea of difficulty estimation as a metacognitive process, as the evidence for the difficulty judgment is given by the output of lower-level decisions, thus instantiating a processing hierarchy.
source: The model makes concrete the idea of difficulty estimation as a metacognitive process, as the evidence for the difficulty judgment is given by the output of lower-level decisions, thus instantiating a processing hierarchy.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the model.

claim: The absolute value of the DV can be approximated by the greater of the competing accumulations in a race model implementation.
source: The absolute value of the DV can be approximated by the greater of the competing accumulations.
evidence: This is a proposed neural implementation mechanism.

claim: Such a process could be extended to difficulty decisions over more than two stimuli.
source: Such a process could be extended to difficulty decisions over more than two stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential extensions of the model.

claim: Responses were faster when the sum of the color strengths was larger even if the difference in difficulty was the same.
source: Specifically, responses were faster, when the sum of the color strengths was larger (i.e., a 'magnitude' effect) even if the difference in difficulty was the same.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The magnitude effect has a parallel in value-based decision making.
source: This effect has a parallel in value-based decision making. For instance, when people choose between two highly desirable items, the decision is faster than when the items are both less desirable, even if the decisions are difficult because the pairs comprise items of approximately equal value (Smith and Krajbich, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The magnitude effect in value-based decision making can be explained by arguing that attention fluctuates between both items under comparison and that attention has a multiplicative effect on the subjective value of the unattended item.
source: This effect can be explained by arguing that attention fluctuates between both items under comparison and that attention has a multiplicative effect on the subjective value of the unattended item (Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Sepulveda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The attention-based explanation for the magnitude effect does not apply in the difficulty judgment task.
source: This explanation does not apply in our case, since we could largely abolish the magnitude effect by informing the participants about the dominant color in each stimulus patch.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data in Experiment 2.

claim: The magnitude effect occurs because DVs on hard-hard trials cross the bounds later than on easy-easy trials.
source: In our task, the magnitude effect occurs, because DVs on hard-hard trials (Figure 4a, orange circle) cross the bounds later than on easy-easy trials (purple circle).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the model structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: When the color dominance is known, the bounds change so that the DV can reach a bound when lingering near the origin.
source: When the color dominance is known (Figure 4b), the bounds change so that the DV can reach a bound when lingering near the origin.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the model structure shown in Figure 4b.

claim: When the color dominance is known, the RTs only depend on difference in difficulty and not the magnitude.
source: Therefore, the RTs now only depend on difference in difficulty and not the magnitude.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The model that maximizes reward rate in the unknown color dominance task qualitatively reproduces the behavior of the participants.
source: The model that maximizes reward rate in our unknown color dominance task (Experiment 1) qualitatively reproduces the behavior of the participants.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the optimal model to participant behavior.

claim: The optimal model shows a similar 'magnitude effect' to that observed in the data and the same criss-cross pattern in response times.
source: In particular, the optimal model shows a similar 'magnitude effect' to that observed in the data and the same criss-cross pattern in response times.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the optimal model to participant behavior.

claim: The magnitude effect and criss-cross pattern in response times do not signify suboptimal decision making.
source: Therefore, these features of the data do not signify suboptimal decision making.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the optimal model analysis.

claim: The model that most closely resembles the optimal model is also the one that best explains the participants' data.
source: That is, the model that most closely resembles the optimal model is also the one that best explains the participants' data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: The optimal model predicts that the speed at which the bounds collapse depend both on elapsed time and the magnitude of the decision variables.
source: The optimal model predicts that the speed at which the bounds collapse depend both on elapsed time and the magnitude of the decision variables (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is a conclusion from analyzing the optimal model shown in Figure 8b.

claim: In the difference model the speed at which the bounds collapse depends only on elapsed time.
source: In contrast, in the difference model the speed at which the bounds collapse depends only on elapsed time.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The results are not affected by whether participants sample the stimulus sequentially through alternation or in a parallel manner.
source: However, our results are not affected by whether participants sample the stimulus sequentially through alternation (which we assume is fast and has equal times for both stimulus) or in a parallel manner (cf., Kang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a methodological clarification supported by a citation.

claim: In the parallel model information is acquired at twice the rate of the serial model.
source: In the parallel model information is acquired at twice the rate of the serial model.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Simple perceptual decision of the type studied have been shown to involve accumulation.
source: Given that simple perceptual decision of the type we study have been shown to involve accumulation, we chose not to consider non-accumulation models (Stine et al., 2020; Cisek et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citations.

claim: It is an open question whether the results from the simple perceptual decision task would generalize to more naturalistic real-world tasks.
source: Third, it is an open question whether the results we obtain from our simple perceptual decision task would generalize to more naturalistic real-world tasks (e.g., choosing an instrument to learn or a recipe to cook).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: The feedback provided on each trial is likely to differ in the real world, where difficulty is rarely directly indicated.
source: Moreover, the feedback we provided on each trial—which of the two tasks was actually easier—is likely to differ in the real world, where difficulty is rarely directly indicated.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Accumulation models have been extended to more complex tasks such as decision making in a game of chess.
source: Importantly, accumulation models have been extended to more complex tasks such as decision making in a game of chess (Fernandez Slezak et al., 2018) and therefore in principle the same types of algorithm could operate for more complex difficulty judgment tasks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: An explicit calculation of confidence in the color decisions is not necessary in the difficulty judgment task.
source: An explicit calculation of confidence in the color decisions is not necessary in our task, because the difficulty decision is based on quantity derived directly from the two color decision variables.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model comparison analysis.

claim: There may be situations where the difficulty determinations involve calculation of confidence as an intermediate step.
source: That said, there may be situations where the difficulty determinations involve calculation of confidence as an intermediate step. For example, in a difficulty comparison of a color dominance in one patch and motion direction in another patch, the decision variables may not be directly comparable and may therefore require a conversion to confidence (de Gardelle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential extensions supported by a citation.

claim: The difference model can explain difficulty judgments in both an RT and controlled duration task.
source: In summary, we have shown that a difference model can explain difficulty judgments in both an RT and controlled duration task and when the dominant color of both patches is either unknown or known.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all experiments.

claim: The results extend decision-making models, which have been used to explain choice, RT, and confidence to judgments of difficulty.
source: The results extend decision-making models, which have been used to explain choice, RT, and confidence to judgments of difficulty.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the contribution of the work.

claim: 51 participants were recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk for Experiment 1.
source: For Experiment 1 (Difficulty judgments in an RT task), 51 participants were recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Only participants who completed the entire study and met performance-based inclusion criteria were included in the final sample of 20 participants for Experiment 1.
source: Only participants who completed the entire study and met performance-based inclusion criteria (see below) were included in the final sample of 20 participants (12 male and 8 female; 19 right-handed; age 20–51, mean = 33.6, sd = 9.1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: For Experiment 2, four participants were recruited via a Sona Systems participant pool.
source: For Experiment 2 (Difficulty judgments with unknown vs. known color dominance), four participants were recruited via a Sona Systems participant pool.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: After initial training, three participants were selected for the main experiment in Experiment 2 based on their performance.
source: After initial training, three participants (one male and two female; all right-handed; age 20–24, mean = 21.7, sd = 2.1) were selected for the main experiment based on their performance (see below).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Both experiments were conducted remotely during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic (summer 2021).
source: Both experiments were conducted remotely during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic (summer 2021).
evidence: This describes the experimental context.

claim: Participants completed the task online using a Google Chrome browser.
source: Participants completed the task online using a Google Chrome browser.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The task was programmed in JavaScript and jsPsych.
source: The task was programmed in JavaScript and jsPsych (de Leeuw, 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and is supported by a citation.

claim: Visual stimuli were presented with a screen refresh rate of 60 Hz.
source: Visual stimuli were presented with a screen refresh rate of 60 Hz and stimulus density of 16 dots/deg2/s (i.e., 4 dots displayed in each aperture on each frame).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: All 12 × 12 color-coherence combinations for the two patches were presented in a pseudo-random, counterbalanced manner during the task.
source: All 12 × 12 color-coherence combinations for the two patches were presented in a pseudo-random, counterbalanced manner during the task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: For correct responses, participants won 1 point.
source: For correct responses, participants won 1 point.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: After errors and miss trials, participants lost 1 point.
source: After errors and miss trials (too early/late), participants lost 1 point.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: For trials in which both stimuli were equally difficult, half of the trials were randomly designated 'correct'.
source: For trials in which both stimuli were equally difficult (i.e., same coherence level), half of the trials were randomly designated 'correct'.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants whose sensitivity (slope parameter of logistic) of color choices was less than 4 were excluded from the experiment.
source: Specifically, participants whose sensitivity (slope parameter of logistic) of color choices was less than 4 (n=4), or whose sensitivity of difficulty choices was less than 3 (n=21) (a lower threshold used here as we found difficulty choices were harder than color choices), were not invited to participate in session 2 and were excluded from all analyses.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria.

claim: Participants whose sensitivity of difficulty choices was less than 3 were excluded from the experiment.
source: Specifically, participants whose sensitivity (slope parameter of logistic) of color choices was less than 4 (n=4), or whose sensitivity of difficulty choices was less than 3 (n=21) (a lower threshold used here as we found difficulty choices were harder than color choices), were not invited to participate in session 2 and were excluded from all analyses.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria.

claim: Exclusion criteria were not based on RT, and instead, were strictly based on accuracy to ensure that participants followed the task instructions correctly.
source: Importantly, exclusion criteria were not based on RT (our main analysis in the study), and instead, were strictly based on accuracy to ensure that participants followed the task instructions correctly.
